title: The India–China reset will continue at the BRICS summit
gist: India hosts the 18th BRICS summit in New Delhi on 12–13 September 2026 while trying to steer the bloc back to a development-and-economics agenda and away from anti-US statements, even as it deepens a China reset via a Modi–Xi bilateral and Xi's first India visit since 2019. The real signal is on the sidelines: bilateral deal-making, border-dispute progress, and a deliberate Indian effort to defuse the de-dollarization narrative that drew Trump's tariff threat.

insights.claim: India's response to strained relations with the second Trump administration has been to reinvest in non-US relationships rather than capitulate, securing resource deals across Australia, Indonesia and Uzbekistan during recent Modi visits while US trade talks drag on.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Indian commodity and energy supply chains are diversifying away from US-aligned channels; watch resource-deal counterparties in Australia and Central Asia for order flow that would otherwise have been US-brokered.
insights.quote: New Delhi secured a string of resource deals during Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s recent visits to Australia, Indonesia and Uzbekistan.
insights.locator: Strain with Washington, reengagement with Moscow and Beijing

insights.claim: India has concluded or has in progress nine trade deals since 2021, including with the United Kingdom and the European Union, giving it a diversified trade base that reduces the leverage of US tariff pressure.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A concrete measure of India's optionality: tariff threats from Washington bite less when nine alternative trade agreements are already in motion.
insights.quote: it has agreed a number of trade deals, with nine in-progress or concluded since 2021 – including with the United Kingdom and European Union
insights.locator: Recent Indian government actions confirm

insights.claim: The rest of the world is now converging on India's longstanding doctrine of strategic autonomy and middle-power hedging, driven by the Ukraine and Iran wars, US–China rivalry and Trump's second term.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect more states to refuse bloc alignment, which raises the value of multi-aligned intermediaries and complicates sanctions enforcement and export-control regimes.
insights.quote: the rest of the world is increasingly seeking to emulate its longstanding policy of strategic autonomy
insights.locator: India will host the 18th BRICS summit

insights.claim: India's abrupt re-engagement with the Shanghai Cooperation Organization marks a real shift: after hosting only a low-key virtual SCO summit in 2023 and Modi skipping the 2024 summit, Modi joined Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in signing the Bishkek Declaration condemning US–Israeli attacks on Iran.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A measurable defection signal from the US-aligned camp; the trajectory of Indian participation in China-led forums is the cleanest read on how far Washington's leverage over Delhi has eroded.
insights.quote: Modi joined President Xi Jinping and President Vladimir Putin in signing the Bishkek Declaration, which condemned US-Israeli military attacks on Iran.
insights.locator: Ony a few years ago, India was distancing itself

insights.claim: New Delhi has explicitly reframed the BRICS de-dollarization agenda as bilateral trade settlement in national currencies plus digital payments to cut cross-border transaction costs, and has publicly denied any effort to create a rival reserve currency.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The near-term threat to dollar reserve status from BRICS is being actively de-escalated by its own chair; the practical exposure is in payment-rails and local-currency settlement infrastructure, not reserve reallocation.
insights.quote: New Delhi emphasized that BRICS is not seeking to create a separate reserve currency to compete with the US dollar.
insights.locator: New Delhi emphasized that BRICS is not seeking

insights.claim: Trump last year threatened to impose ten per cent tariffs on BRICS countries in response to the de-dollarization narrative championed by Brazil and Russia, establishing a concrete tariff trigger tied to currency rhetoric.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A defined, priced policy reaction function: any summit language reviving reserve-currency ambitions is a live tariff catalyst for BRICS-exposed exporters.
insights.quote: an idea which last year caused President Trump to threaten to slap ten per cent tariffs on the BRICS in response
insights.locator: That includes a de-dollarization narrative

themes.theme: BRICS identity crisis and cohesion risk

insights.claim: Two decades after formation, the four founding BRICS states still have no consensus on the bloc's purpose: Brazil and India treat it as an economics-driven initiative while China and Russia see it through a geopolitical lens.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: This split caps the bloc's ability to produce binding economic architecture; discount headlines about BRICS as a coordinated economic counterweight.
insights.quote: Brazil and India see it primarily as an economic-driven initiative. China and Russia see it through more of a geopolitical lens.
insights.locator: Additionally, among the founding member states

insights.claim: Cohesion among the 11 BRICS member states is undermined by multiple live intra-bloc disputes — Iran versus the UAE over the Middle East conflict, Ethiopia versus Egypt over the Nile dam, and conflicting Saudi and UAE positions on Israel.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Enlargement diluted rather than strengthened the bloc; expect communiqué-level output only, and do not price in coordinated BRICS action on energy or sanctions.
insights.quote: Relations between Addis Ababa and Cairo have been strained by Ethiopia’s Nile dam project.
insights.locator: Multilateral symbolism

insights.claim: BRICS expansion is likely to take a backseat for the foreseeable future, with the focus shifting to socializing existing new members and limited engagement with other Global South forums.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Accession speculation for candidate states is a low-probability trade through the next cycle; positioning should assume a static 11-member bloc.
insights.quote: Such factors mean that BRICS expansion is likely to take a backseat for the foreseeable future.
insights.locator: Such factors mean that BRICS expansion

insights.claim: Small, exclusive regional groupings such as the recent defence pact between Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia may become more consequential actors than expansive, inclusive groupings like BRICS.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Track minilateral defence and trade pacts rather than headline summits for where alignment risk and defence procurement flows are actually forming.
insights.quote: There is a possibility that such regional, exclusive groupings may become more important actors than expansive and inclusive groupings like BRICS.
insights.locator: In the two decades since the BRICS was formed

insights.claim: The Global South remains an amorphous concept with little clarity on what advocating its interests means beyond vague calls for a more equitable multipolar distribution of power.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Treat 'Global South' framing in policy communiqués as rhetoric with low predictive value for actual capital flows or institutional change.
insights.quote: Ultimately, the Global South remains an amorphous concept.
insights.locator: Ultimately, the Global South remains

insights.claim: China is increasingly using BRICS to propagate its own Global Development, Security, Civilization and Governance Initiatives, while Russia uses it to court the Global South while ostracized by the West over Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: BRICS output should be read as a Chinese norm-setting channel; watch for Chinese governance-initiative language entering summit texts as a marker of Beijing's institutional reach.
insights.quote: Beijing in particular is increasingly using forums like the BRICS to promote its own worldviews through its Global Development, Security, Civilization and Governance Initiatives.
insights.locator: Beijing in particular is increasingly using forums

themes.theme: India–China reset: the real deal flow

insights.claim: The substantive outcomes of the New Delhi BRICS summit will come from sideline bilaterals rather than the plenary, with the Modi–Xi meeting expected to advance the India–China reset and build confidence.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Trade the bilateral readouts, not the communiqué; India–China normalization has direct implications for border trade, rare-earth and component supply, and Indian manufacturing input costs.
insights.quote: The real action at the BRICS Summit will take place on its sidelines with a series of bilateral meetings.
insights.locator: Bilateral substance

insights.claim: Xi Jinping's upcoming visit to India will be his first since 2019 and is reported to include a 400-person delegation, an unusually large business-and-officials footprint signalling substantive intent behind the reset.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Delegation size of that scale usually precedes commercial agreements; watch for Chinese investment, supply-chain and visa liberalization announcements around the visit.
insights.quote: Xi’s upcoming visit to India – his first since 2019 – will reportedly include a 400-person delegation
insights.locator: And Xi’s upcoming visit to India

insights.claim: An August meeting between the Chinese foreign minister and India's national security advisor made notable progress on the longstanding border dispute, the most concrete de-escalation marker in the reset.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Border risk premium on India–China economic exposure is falling; a durable border framework would unlock direct investment flows currently blocked on security grounds.
insights.quote: A meeting in August between the Chinese foreign minister and Indian national security advisor made notable progress on their longstanding border dispute.
insights.locator: A meeting in August between the Chinese foreign minister

insights.claim: BRICS's principal remaining value is convening power rather than policy output — it was a Modi–Xi meeting at the 2024 BRICS summit in Russia that started the India–China reset.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Value these summits as scheduling infrastructure for bilaterals; the tradable events are the meetings they make possible, not the declarations they issue.
insights.quote: The recent accomplishments of BRICS have come from its convening power.
insights.locator: The recent accomplishments of BRICS

themes.theme: India's chairmanship agenda and its key risk

insights.claim: The central watchpoint at the New Delhi summit is whether India, as chair, can avoid overseeing a Bishkek-style statement condemning US military action, since it is trying to stay on good terms with Washington while other members demand opposition to US strikes on Iran and Venezuela.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The summit communiqué's language on US strikes is the binary risk event: a condemnation revives Trump's BRICS tariff threat and reprices Indian export exposure.
insights.quote: As Chair and host of BRICS, India’s actions will be more scrutinized, and it will be reluctant to oversee the production of a statement similar to Bishkek.
insights.locator: A key watchpoint at this summit

insights.claim: India's BRICS chairmanship has produced three concrete deliverables — the August 'Chennai Consensus' on collaborative emerging-technology research among developing countries, a BRICS trade ministers' push to preserve the multilateral trading system aimed at Trump's tariff policies, and a June agriculture ministers' food security declaration.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Shows the agenda India wants: tech cooperation, trade-system defence and agriculture — the areas where BRICS outputs are most likely to carry real commercial follow-through.
insights.quote: In August a joint declaration, the ‘ Chennai Consensus ’ made a commitment to collaborative research and innovation among developing countries on emerging technologies.
insights.locator: India’s BRICS agenda

insights.claim: India will use the summit to push BRICS back toward its founding development agenda via an Economic Partnership Strategy 2030, building on the 2015 New Development Bank and Contingent Reserve Arrangement, but this risks being hijacked by member fissures and demands for another anti-US statement.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: If the Economic Partnership Strategy 2030 survives the summit intact, development-finance channels through the New Development Bank become the more investable BRICS vector.
insights.quote: At the summit, New Delhi will seek to return BRICS to its original development-focused agenda, as reflected in its Economic Partnership Strategy 2030 .
insights.locator: At the summit, New Delhi will seek to return

insights.claim: India's benign 'Humanity First' BRICS framing already looks outdated against US military action on Venezuela and Iran, and Delhi's non-Western-but-not-anti-Western positioning is out of sync with members like China, Russia and Iran plus Brazil and South Africa, both of which have had high-profile diplomatic disputes with Washington.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: India is the marginal moderating vote inside an increasingly adversarial bloc; if its restraint fails, BRICS re-rates as a confrontational body and US tariff risk to all members rises.
insights.quote: India’s position can appear out of sync in a forum whose membership includes countries with more overtly anti-Western agendas, including China, Russia and Iran.
insights.locator: But this seems increasingly outdated

insights.claim: Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rehman, whose country chairs the BIMSTEC regional forum, has not yet accepted India's summit invitation amid bilateral tensions, showing that even India's modest plan to expand the BRICS mandate through Global South forum engagement is running into friction.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: India–Bangladesh friction is a live constraint on Delhi's regional convening power and on South Asian connectivity projects routed through BIMSTEC.
insights.quote: Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rehman – whose country holds the chair of BIMSTEC, a South and Southeast Asian regional forum – has not yet accepted an invitation amid tensions with India.
insights.locator: However, even this is challenging
